title: Dacryocystitis: Clinical Excellence & Surgical Mastery
summary: A comprehensive deep-dive into the pathogenesis, diagnosis, and management of lacrimal sac inflammation. This guide covers everything from the microbiology of acute infections to the intricate steps of Dacryocystorhinostomy (DCR).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Dacryocystitis is the inflammation and infection of the lacrimal sac, almost invariably occurring secondary to obstruction of the nasolacrimal duct (NLDO). It is characterized by a bimodal age distribution and presents as either an acute, life-threatening orbital emergency or a chronic, smoldering condition causing persistent epiphora and discharge. Effective management requires a combination of aggressive antimicrobial therapy and definitive surgical bypass of the obstruction.

rows: S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, B-hemolytic Strep

sections.title: Pathophysiology Flow
content: Step 1: Nasolacrimal Duct Obstruction (NLDO) - Primary (PANDO) or Secondary (Stone, Trauma).
Step 2: Stasis of Tear Film - Accumulation of tears, debris, and bacteria within the lacrimal sac.
Step 3: Bacterial Proliferation - Stagnant environment promotes rapid growth of normal skin/conjunctival flora.
Step 4: Mucosal Inflammation - Edema and hypervascularity of the sac lining.
Step 5: Abscess Formation - High pressure leads to sac distension and potential rupture into surrounding tissue.

sections.title: Essential Diagnostic Workup
content: External Exam: Check for swelling BELOW the medial canthal tendon (suggests sac vs tumor).
Regurgitation Test: Pressure on sac produces mucoid/purulent reflux from puncta.
Jones I Test: Fluorescein recovery in the nose (negative in obstruction).
Jones II Test: Syringing/Irrigation to identify the site of obstruction.
Probing: Determines 'Hard Stop' (bone/NLD) vs 'Soft Stop' (canalicular obstruction).
Culture/Sensitivity: Vital for selecting narrow-spectrum antibiotics.

sections.title: The DCR Surgical Blueprint
content: 1. Incision: 10-12mm linear incision 8mm medial to inner canthus (External) or Endonasal approach.
2. Exposure: Dissection through orbicularis to reach the medial canthal tendon and lacrimal crest.
3. Periosteal Elevation: Reflecting the lacrimal sac laterally to expose the lacrimal fossa.
4. Osteotomy: Creating a 15mm bone window using a Kerrison Rongeur or drill (removing lacrimal bone and maxilla).
5. Intubation: Passing Bowman probes/Crawford stents through puncta into the nasal cavity.
6. Flap Creation: H-shaped incisions in sac mucosa and nasal mucosa to create anterior/posterior flaps.
7. Anastomosis: Suturing flaps (usually 6-0 Vicryl) to create a permanent bypass track.
8. Closure: Skin closure with 6-0 Prolene or fast-absorbing gut.

sections.title: Emergency Red Flags
content: Orbital Cellulitis: Proptosis, ophthalmoplegia, and decreased vision.
Cavernous Sinus Thrombosis: Bilateral involvement, CN palsies, rapid progression.
Meningitis: Nuchal rigidity, altered mental status.
Sac Abscess Pointing: Spontaneous skin fistulization risk.
Non-resolving Swelling: Suspicion of Lacrimal Sac Squamous Cell Carcinoma.

sections.title: Medical Management Protocol
content: Acute Phase: Warm compresses and digital massage (Crigler maneuver).
Oral Antibiotics: Amoxicillin/Clavulanate (Augmentin) 875mg BID or Cephalexin 500mg QID.
Severe/Febrile: IV Cefazolin or Vancomycin (if MRSA suspected).
Analgesia: NSAIDs (Ibuprofen 400-600mg) for pain and inflammation.
Avoid Irrigation: Never syring/probe during acute infection (risk of spreading sepsis).

sections.title: Landmark Studies & Advances
content: Endonasal vs. External: Meta-analyses show equivalent success rates (approx. 90-95%) in experienced hands.
Mitomycin-C (MMC): Use of 0.02% MMC on osteotomy site may reduce ostium cicatrization.
Lacrimal Scintigraphy: Emerging as the gold standard for 'Functional' NLDO vs 'Anatomical'.
Dacryocystoplasty: Balloon dilation is increasingly used for partial stenoses before committing to DCR.

content.explanation: Jones 1 (Primary): If Fluorescein appears in nose after 5 mins, system is patent (Fun!). Jones 2 (Secondary): If syringing forces fluorescein into nose, it was a functional block. If clear saline, it's a complete anatomical block (True blockage).

sections.title: Post-Operative Complications
content: Hemorrhage: Severe epistaxis (often from the angular vein or sphenopalatine artery).
Stent Prolapse: Crawford tubes looping out of the medial canthus.
Cicatricial Failure: Ostium closure due to excessive scarring.
Cerebrospinal Fluid (CSF) Leak: Rare, caused by accidental ethmoid roof penetration.
Canalicular Cheese-wiring: Stents cutting through the punctal tissue.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls for Residents
content: A mucocele is sterile; a dacryocystitis is infected. Treat the infection before the surgery.
Always palpate for the medial canthal tendon. If the mass is above the tendon, think MALIGNANCY until proven otherwise.
In congenital cases, 90% resolve by age 1 with massage. Do not rush to probe unless dacryocystocele (amnentocele) is present.
Check the nose! 15% of DCR failures are due to unrecognized nasal pathology (septal deviation, polyps, or synechiae).
